value.overview: The Mealy Amazon is a large, mostly green parrot of tropical Central and South America. It is named for the pale, powdery or “mealy” appearance created by bluish-gray shading across its back and nape. Usually found high in the forest canopy, it may be difficult to see despite its loud calls. Pairs and small flocks travel between feeding areas, while much larger groups may gather at abundant food sources, clay licks, and communal roosts.
value.classification: The Mealy Amazon belongs to the parrot order Psittaciformes and family Psittacidae. It is a member of the Neotropical amazon parrot genus Amazona.
value.identification: A large, heavy-bodied amazon parrot, the Mealy Amazon measures about 38–41 centimeters long. Its plumage is predominantly green, with a dusty bluish-gray wash over the nape and upper back. Some birds have scattered yellow feathers on the crown. The wings show red on the leading edge and secondary feathers, most visible in flight. It has a pale horn-colored bill, a broad bare whitish eye-ring, and reddish eyes in adults. Juveniles generally have darker brown eyes.
value.rangeHabitat: Under the eBird/Clements treatment used by Bird Intel, the Mealy Amazon includes northern forms from southeastern Mexico through Central America to western Panama and southern populations from eastern Panama through much of tropical South America. Costa Rica is occupied by the northern form traditionally called the Costa Rican or Green-headed Mealy Amazon, Amazona farinosa virenticeps. It is a resident of humid lowland and foothill forest, forest edge, and wooded plantations where large canopy trees remain available for feeding, roosting, and nesting.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident and nonmigratory, although flocks make local or seasonal movements in response to changing food availability.
value.breeding: Breeding timing varies across the wide range, with nesting reported from November to March in parts of Brazil and during other months elsewhere. Mealy Amazons form monogamous pairs and nest in natural cavities in living trees or dead palms. A typical clutch contains about three white eggs. The female performs most or all incubation for roughly four weeks while the male brings her regurgitated food. Both parents feed the chicks, which usually leave the nest after approximately eight to ten weeks.
value.dietFeeding: Mealy Amazons eat mainly fruits, seeds, nuts, berries, flowers, buds, arils, and nectar gathered in the upper forest canopy. Figs, palms, legumes, and many other tropical trees provide food. The birds use their strong bills to open hard fruits and seeds and may hold food with one foot while eating. Flocks sometimes visit maize fields or other cultivated areas. At some sites they gather at exposed mineral-rich soil or clay licks.
value.behavior: These parrots are commonly seen in pairs or flocks of up to about 20 birds, with larger gatherings where food is plentiful. Outside the breeding season, hundreds may assemble at traditional communal roosts in tall trees. They are social, noisy in flight, and produce deep screams, squawks, whistles, chatter, and babbling calls. While feeding quietly among canopy foliage, their green plumage provides effective camouflage. Pairs maintain close contact and often travel together within larger flocks.

conservation.populationTrend: Decreasing. Current conservation authorities often assess the northern Mealy Amazon group, which includes the Costa Rican population, separately from southern populations.
conservation.threats: Loss and fragmentation of mature forest, removal of large nesting trees, and capture for the illegal parrot trade are important pressures.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect mature lowland and foothill forest, retain large cavity-bearing trees, avoid buying wild-caught parrots, and support local habitat protection and monitoring programs.
